properties.digitization_method: REDONE 2026-09-14: the diagram-transform version of this polygon (described below, kept for history) placed Building 2 entirely on the paved road median of Illinois St -- confirmed wrong against satellite imagery (no structure there at all). User pointed out the real match is not the warehouse building across the street, but the large vacant/graded lot on the WEST side of Illinois St, between roughly 20th and 21st St -- its silhouette (elongated, tilted a few degrees off true north, matching the local curb bearing) is the same shape being traced, just larger. Re-traced directly from that lot's own visible boundary: anchored on two points read off the lot's real east edge (the Illinois St curb, high-contrast and unambiguous), which gave a measured bearing of ~182.3/272.3 degrees. CORRECTED same day: user caught that this made the east edge visibly non-parallel to the real curb -- the two curb points used for that bearing were only ~13m apart (an 80m along-curb baseline but just ~3.5m of east-west offset between them), so a 1-2 pixel misreading at zoom 20 (~0.3-0.6m each) was enough to swing the derived bearing by several degrees -- exactly the 'reading points too close together, small errors don't cancel' failure this project's bearing_trace.py already warns about, repeated instead of heeded. Fixed by using this site's already-established, multiply-validated grid bearing (176.5/356.5 degrees, from Historic Building 14's real surveyed footprint, and consistent with Block B's own independently-confirmed ~175 degrees) instead of re-deriving a fresh one from a short noisy baseline; kept the same real anchor point and the same independently-measured distances (~126m north-south, ~51m east-west). SECOND CORRECTION, same day: user caught that the resulting rectangle still overlapped the street -- the anchor point itself (read near a crosswalk with parked cars and shadow clutter) was actually ~8-9m INSIDE the road, not on the curb, even though the bearing was by then correct. Root cause: misread the sidewalk/asphalt color transition in a cluttered spot. Re-read the curb at two clean, unobstructed points well clear of any crosswalk (via a brightness-transition scan of the sidewalk-to-asphalt boundary at zoom 20, cross-checked against the pixel-to-lonlat math directly rather than by eye), which independently reproduced the same 176.57 degree bearing (confirming the established bearing was never the problem) but placed the curb about 8.5m further west than the previous anchor. Extrapolated the corrected curb line to the same north/south extents and rebuilt the west edge at the same 51m width. Overlay-checked both the north and south corners individually afterward: the east edge now sat on the sidewalk side of the curb along its whole length, not on the asphalt. THIRD CORRECTION, same day: user pointed out the east edge was still at the OUTER (curb) side of the public Illinois St sidewalk, meaning the polygon's area included the whole ~4.5m-wide public sidewalk itself, not just the private lot -- and that the south edge (the cross-street's own sidewalk/crosswalk) had the identical problem, cutting straight through the crosswalk stripe pattern rather than stopping at the back of that sidewalk. Fixed both: re-read the INNER (lot-side/back-of-sidewalk) edge of the Illinois St sidewalk, at the dirt-to-concrete color transition on the lot side rather than the concrete-to-asphalt transition on the street side (found ~4.5m west of the previous curb-line anchor, at the same validated 176.5 degree bearing -- confirms this project's east edges up to now, including PKN/PKS/E1/E2/HDY3 etc., were anchored on curbs; worth re-checking whether any of those also failed to exclude a real sidewalk). Re-read the south edge similarly: found the true back-of-sidewalk transition on the lot side of the cross-street's own sidewalk (north of its crosswalk stripes, not through them) and rebuilt the south edge through that point, perpendicular to the same established bearing, solving for new SE/SW corners as the intersection with the (unchanged) east and west edge lines. Overlay-confirmed the south edge now runs clear of the crosswalk stripes along its whole length. FOURTH CORRECTION (negligible, ~0.17m): when generalizing this fix into a reusable, tested function (bearing_trace.rectangle_from_four_edges, added along with src/test_bearing_trace.py), recomputing NE from the same raw measured anchors gave a corner ~0.17m from the hand-computed one above (accumulated rounding across several manual correction passes) -- adjusted NE to match the function's output exactly, so the file and the tested reconstruction agree bit-for-bit rather than by coincidence. See src/test_bearing_trace.py for the from-scratch reconstruction this geometry must continue to match. NOTE: this lot is visibly larger (~126m x 51m) than Warehouse No. 2's documented 236ft x 76ft (~72m x 23m) footprint, and satellite imagery shows no internal boundary, fence, or foundation distinguishing a smaller building footprint within it -- the lot currently reads as a single, undivided vacant/graded surface, which is actually consistent with this file's own (previously contradictory) accuracy_caveat text describing 'vacant/graded land,' despite regulatory_context describing Warehouse No. 2 as an existing historic structure. This polygon is therefore the best satellite-confirmable placeholder (the real, shared lot the building's documented footprint sits within) but is NOT a precise building footprint -- treat it as an upper bound on Building 2's true location, not the building's actual extent, and treat the 'historic structure, existing' status in this file with caution pending a source that resolves the discrepancy. Overlaps Parcels C1 and C2 (860 m2 and 1035 m2) in this project's own overlap QA -- not clipped, because all three are approximate placeholders competing for the same currently-undivided vacant lot; clipping any of them against another would not make any of them more accurate. See C1/C2's own accuracy_caveat for the matching note. Prior diagram-transform method (for history): traced from the Pier 70 Design for Development's own Figure 6.4.2 (Maximum Building Height, p.155) -- an adopted regulatory diagram with a printed scale bar, north arrow, and real street labels, not an illustrative rendering. Georeferenced using 5 real street-intersection control points (Illinois St and Michigan St, each crossing 20th St and 21st St) fetched from OpenStreetMap via this project's own src/fetch_streets.py, plus the real, independently-confirmed position of Historic Building 12 (blklot 4114010) as a 6th anchor, fit as a least-squares affine transform. Residual error against the fitted control points is roughly 8-25m -- wider than Mission Rock's equivalent transform (which had more, better-distributed real street intersections available). RELOCATED 2026-09-16 (full Pier 70 geometry restart): the west-lot placement above is WRONG, not just imprecise. Root cause: this project's own D4D research had already surfaced that Building 21's sourcing describes 'the historic node of Buildings 2, 12, and 21' (Figure 3.6.1's caption) -- i.e. Building 2 should sit immediately next to the real, confirmed positions of Building 12 (blklot 4114010) and Building 21 (re-traced 2026-09-16), on the EAST side of the site near Maryland St. It does not; Figure 6.4.2 itself confirms this directly, showing a gray 'Historic Building' box labeled plainly '2' immediately next to the 'D' and '12' boxes in that same east cluster -- not anywhere near Illinois St/C1/C2 where the west-lot version was placed. The west-lot placement was a guess made without checking this: it was chosen only because it was the nearest large satellite-visible vacant/graded surface west of Illinois St, without cross-referencing the diagram's own explicit label placement for '2', and without noticing that a 126m x 51m 'whole shared lot' was already flagged in this very file as 4x larger than Warehouse No. 2's documented 236ft x 76ft footprint -- a mismatch that should have been the tell. Re-traced this block's real position directly: isolated the gray 'Historic Building' legend color (RGB [148,150,153]) in the east cluster, extracted a clean rectangular contour (OpenCV) at pixel (1140,737)-(1206,961), and converted via the same validated 6-point affine transform used for Building 21 and the numbered parcels. Resulting area (~15,235 sqft) is a close match (85%) to the documented 236ft x 76ft (~17,936 sqft) footprint -- strong independent confirmation this is the right building, unlike the west-lot version's 4x-oversized mismatch. Confirmed zero overlap with Building 21, Parcel D, or Building 12 Plaza. The former west-lot placement's own extensive correction history (five passes, all satellite-based) is kept below for the record, but none of that work applies to this building's real position -- it was carefully refining the wrong location. 2026-09-29 accuracy audit: the Assessor fact (Building 12 at blklot 4114010) and the OpenStreetMap street control points above are our own lookups (DataSF Assessor parcels layer; OSM via src/fetch_streets.py), not statements in the D4D, which this file cites for the diagram and Building 2's dimensions. Nothing in the geometry was changed. 2026-10-02: public-text pass. accuracy_caveat, why_no_real_parcel, notes reworded for readers (meaning unchanged; no change to the shape, status, use or geometry_type); previous wording -- accuracy_caveat: 'APPROXIMATE -- RELOCATED 2026-09-16 from an incorrect west-lot placement (see digitization_method) to Figure 6.4.2's own labeled '2' Historic Building box, in the same east-side node as Buildings 12 and 21. Programmatically traced from this legend color, not hand-verified vertex-by-vertex; treat vertex positions as accurate to roughly 5-15m, consistent with this site's other diagram-traced parcels. The close match (85%) between this trace's area and Warehouse No. 2's documented 236ft x 76ft footprint is a good independent sanity check, but this is still a simplified rectangle, not a surveyed building outline.'; why_no_real_parcel: 'Not matched to a specific Assessor lot. DataSF's Assessor layer (repo copy data/raw/parcels.geojson) shows the Pier 70 28-acre site re-mapped into many active P70-MU lots in blocks 4052 and 4110-4117 (mostly added 2019-02-07), so the earlier statement that it has not been subdivided is withdrawn; which lot corresponds to this block has not been checked against the recorded final map, so this file uses hand-traced approximate geometry instead.'; notes: 'Approximate polygon for a real, D4D-adopted parcel -- see accuracy_caveat.'.
properties.accuracy_caveat: APPROXIMATE -- RELOCATED 2026-09-16 from an incorrect west-lot placement (logged, with the rest of this shape's history, in its data file in the public data repository, https://github.com/pierandpoint/record) to Figure 6.4.2's own labeled '2' Historic Building box, in the same east-side node as Buildings 12 and 21. properties.why_no_real_parcel: Not matched to a specific Assessor lot. DataSF's Assessor layer shows the Pier 70 28-acre site re-mapped into many active P70-MU lots in blocks 4052 and 4110-4117 (mostly added 2019-02-07), so the earlier statement that it has not been subdivided is withdrawn; which lot corresponds to this block has not been checked against the recorded final map, so this record uses hand-traced approximate geometry instead.
properties.regulatory_context: Officially 'Warehouse No. 2' per the D4D (Section 6.6.1), a historic industrial shop structure, footprint 236 ft x 76 ft. Its use is not settled: the D4D treats it as a flexible parcel (Figure 2.1.1 stripes it Commercial-Office/Residential; the land-use scenarios in Figures 1.5.5-1.5.7 show it Residential in the Mid-Point baseline and Maximum Residential and Commercial-Office in Maximum Office), a 2021 development-agreement filing summarised about 120 dwelling units (SF YIMBY), and Brookfield's leasing page (pier70sf.com/leasing) shows 'creative office'. The NRHP gross area is 98,804 sq ft; a ~100,000 RSF brochure figure and a '~50,000 GSF, Arts/Maker' description formerly recorded here are uncited and have been dropped. No source found confirms whether rehabilitation has started; absent from the Port's own June 2025 progress update.

properties.digitization_method: SPLIT 2026-09-16 from the combined blklot 4046001 row (previously one polygon covering Buildings 101, 102, 104, 122, and 123 together, since the real Assessor lot has no further official subdivision -- see status.csv history). properties.digitized_from: Potrero Power Station Design for Development, Figure 6.2.3 - Building Height Plan (p.245).
properties.digitization_method: Traced from the Potrero Power Station Design for Development's own Figure 6.2.3 (Building Height Plan, p.245) -- an adopted regulatory diagram with a printed scale bar, north arrow, and real street labels (Illinois St, Georgia St, Louisiana St, Maryland St, Delaware St, 22nd St, Humboldt St, 23rd St), not an illustrative rendering. Georeferenced using 9 real street-intersection control points fetched from OpenStreetMap via this project's own src/fetch_streets.py, fit as a least-squares affine transform. NOTE: an initial attempt also used the real, confirmed positions of the Sophie Maxwell Building and the UCSF Block 2 building as anchors, but they produced 50-60m of error against the street-only fit -- this diagram is dated Feb 26, 2020, predating UCSF's ~2023-24 arrival as a life-science anchor tenant, so those two real buildings likely do not sit where this 2020 figure's own numbered blocks would place them (their own real parcels are used directly elsewhere in this dataset and were NOT re-derived from this diagram). The final transform here uses street intersections only. Residual error against those control points is roughly 8-24m. Traced polygons were additionally clipped against the real, confirmed Sophie Maxwell and UCSF Block 2 parcels (and against Prequel Park's approximate geometry) so this speculative tracing never overrides real or better-sourced geometry. CORRECTED 2026-09-16: user-flagged pattern of blocks encroaching on real streets across the site (Block 3, Block 11, Block 12) led to rebuilding this whole block layer from scratch using proper GCP-based georeferencing (GDAL's gdaltransform with a thin-plate-spline transform, the same technique QGIS's Georeferencer uses) instead of patching individual curbs. Installed GDAL, computed 8 real street-intersection ground control points from OpenStreetMap data (Craig Lane x Maryland St, 22nd St x Maryland/Louisiana St, Humboldt St x Maryland/Delaware/Georgia Lane, 23rd St x Maryland/Georgia Lane), precisely located each in the source diagram (Figure 6.2.3) via programmatic black-pixel border detection cross-checked with visual ruler crops, and fit a TPS transform. Re-traced this block's own corner pixels the same way and ran them through the new transform. This corrected transform disagrees with the original 9-point affine transform by tens of meters in places -- e.g. it revealed the original trace had Blocks 3/4 shifted east into the excavation pit/street area, and Blocks 11/12 roughly 2x too deep -- and the new positions now land within real, distinct site features (buildings, graded lots) visible in satellite imagery rather than straddling roads. Known residual limitation: GCP street positions are centerline-based (matching OSM convention), while a block boundary should sit at the near curb, so any edge close to a GCP street can land a few meters into that street after transformation -- checked for and corrected on this block's street-facing edge(s) where applicable using this project's already-established grid bearing (356.5 deg) and, where available, an independently diagram-measured depth/width. Treat corrected vertex positions as accurate to roughly 10-15m (tighter than the original 8-24m transform, but still not survey-grade). RE-CORRECTED 2026-09-16 (same day, third pass): the independent per-block TPS re-trace (see above) still measured each block's own 4 corners in isolation, which -- despite using the same transform -- left small (3-12m) spurious gaps or misalignments at boundaries the diagram actually draws as shared or tightly-spaced between adjacent blocks (caught after the user pointed out the diagram itself has ~zero wasted space and specifically that the PG&E switchyard polygon sits directly against Block 5 in the diagram, not ~60m away as this dataset had it). The final transform here uses street intersections only. Residual error against those control points is roughly 8-24m. Traced polygons were additionally clipped against the real, confirmed Sophie Maxwell and UCSF Block 2 parcels (and against Prequel Park's approximate geometry) so this speculative tracing never overrides real or better-sourced geometry. Since the yard here has no visible dirt/pavement curb to measure, used the building's own roofline (measured at two points 33m apart) as a hard constraint, with a 3m clearance -- this only guaranteed no more building overlap, not that the edge sat at the street's true curb. SECOND PASS: user re-flagged the block as still eating the street even after that fix. Went back to the source diagram (Figure 6.2.3) and measured it directly against its own printed scale bar -- this block's own north-south depth (from its shared boundary with Power Station Park to 23rd Street) is roughly 100px at the diagram's ~0.99px/ft scale, i.e. about 31m. This block's committed depth (north edge to first-pass south edge) was 66-67m, more than DOUBLE the diagram's own dimension -- meaning the original diagram-transform trace was badly wrong in an entirely different way than the curb question (a shape/scale error, not just a position error), and no amount of satellite curb-hunting on the south edge could have fixed it, since the real problem was the block being stretched roughly 2x too deep in the first place. Rebuilt the south edge by keeping the (unmodified, more trustworthy) north edge corners fixed and moving south exactly 30.8m along the established 356.5 deg grid bearing, matching the diagram's own measured depth. Note: this block's WIDTH also disagrees with the diagram (currently ~55m vs a diagram-implied ~92m) -- NOT corrected in this pass since it would require moving the east or west edge (shared boundaries with other features not re-verified here); flagged as a known follow-up. CORRECTED 2026-09-16: user-flagged pattern of blocks encroaching on real streets across the site (Block 3, Block 11, Block 12) led to rebuilding this whole block layer from scratch using proper GCP-based georeferencing (GDAL's gdaltransform with a thin-plate-spline transform, the same technique QGIS's Georeferencer uses) instead of patching individual curbs. Installed GDAL, computed 8 real street-intersection ground control points from OpenStreetMap data (Craig Lane x Maryland St, 22nd St x Maryland/Louisiana St, Humboldt St x Maryland/Delaware/Georgia Lane, 23rd St x Maryland/Georgia Lane), precisely located each in the source diagram (Figure 6.2.3) via programmatic black-pixel border detection cross-checked with visual ruler crops, and fit a TPS transform. Re-traced this block's own corner pixels the same way and ran them through the new transform. This corrected transform disagrees with the original 9-point affine transform by tens of meters in places -- e.g. it revealed the original trace had Blocks 3/4 shifted east into the excavation pit/street area, and Blocks 11/12 roughly 2x too deep -- and the new positions now land within real, distinct site features (buildings, graded lots) visible in satellite imagery rather than straddling roads. Known residual limitation: GCP street positions are centerline-based (matching OSM convention), while a block boundary should sit at the near curb, so any edge close to a GCP street can land a few meters into that street after transformation -- checked for and corrected on this block's street-facing edge(s) where applicable using this project's already-established grid bearing (356.5 deg) and, where available, an independently diagram-measured depth/width. Treat corrected vertex positions as accurate to roughly 10-15m (tighter than the original 8-24m transform, but still not survey-grade). RE-CORRECTED 2026-09-16 (same day, third pass): the independent per-block TPS re-trace (see above) still measured each block's own 4 corners in isolation, which -- despite using the same transform -- left small (3-12m) spurious gaps or misalignments at boundaries the diagram actually draws as shared or tightly-spaced between adjacent blocks (caught after the user pointed out the diagram itself has ~zero wasted space and specifically that the PG&E switchyard polygon sits directly against Block 5 in the diagram, not ~60m away as this dataset had it). Re-measured EVERY block's corners in a single consistent pass using programmatic black-pixel border detection (long contiguous runs = real borders, filtered from text/dimension-arrow strokes by requiring the run to span nearly the full block height/width), cross-validated with fine-pixel-gridline crops, so that shared or consistently-measured boundaries between neighboring blocks now come from the same underlying pixel measurements rather than independent eyeball estimates. Batch-transformed through the same GDAL/TPS fit as before. This pass also corrected several block extents that were measured imprecisely in the prior pass (e.g. Block 5's real stepped/notched south edge, Block 11's true position -- it does NOT sit flush against Block 15, there is real Power Station Park open space between them). GCP CORRECTION 2026-09-16 (fourth pass): user flagged that Block 8/12 should touch Delaware Street with park space between them, and that Block 3/4's shapes looked off -- investigation found the root cause was a single mis-measured ground control point. The 'Delaware St x Humboldt St' GCP used for the whole site's TPS transform had been placed at pixel (2227, 986), which is actually deep inside Building 9's own footprint in the diagram, not on Delaware Street at all -- confirmed by comparing pixel spacing between the three Humboldt-row GCPs (Maryland/Delaware/Georgia Lane): Maryland-to-Georgia-Lane's pixel:real-world ratio implied Delaware should sit at roughly pixel x=2020, not 2227, and a direct color-transition scan at y=986 confirmed the real street gap is at x=1994-2035. properties.digitization_method: Traced from the Potrero Power Station Design for Development's own Figure 6.2.3 (Building Height Plan, p.245) -- an adopted regulatory diagram with a printed scale bar, north arrow, and real street labels (Illinois St, Georgia St, Louisiana St, Maryland St, Delaware St, 22nd St, Humboldt St, 23rd St), not an illustrative rendering. Georeferenced using 9 real street-intersection control points fetched from OpenStreetMap via this project's own src/fetch_streets.py, fit as a least-squares affine transform. NOTE: an initial attempt also used the real, confirmed positions of the Sophie Maxwell Building and the UCSF Block 2 building as anchors, but they produced 50-60m of error against the street-only fit -- this diagram is dated Feb 26, 2020, predating UCSF's ~2023-24 arrival as a life-science anchor tenant, so those two real buildings likely do not sit where this 2020 figure's own numbered blocks would place them (their own real parcels are used directly elsewhere in this dataset and were NOT re-derived from this diagram). The final transform here uses street intersections only. Residual error against those control points is roughly 8-24m. Traced polygons were additionally clipped against the real, confirmed Sophie Maxwell and UCSF Block 2 parcels (and against Prequel Park's approximate geometry) so this speculative tracing never overrides real or better-sourced geometry. CORRECTED 2026-09-16: user-flagged pattern of blocks encroaching on real streets across the site (Block 3, Block 11, Block 12) led to rebuilding this whole block layer from scratch using proper GCP-based georeferencing (GDAL's gdaltransform with a thin-plate-spline transform, the same technique QGIS's Georeferencer uses) instead of patching individual curbs. Installed GDAL, computed 8 real street-intersection ground control points from OpenStreetMap data (Craig Lane x Maryland St, 22nd St x Maryland/Louisiana St, Humboldt St x Maryland/Delaware/Georgia Lane, 23rd St x Maryland/Georgia Lane), precisely located each in the source diagram (Figure 6.2.3) via programmatic black-pixel border detection cross-checked with visual ruler crops, and fit a TPS transform. Re-traced this block's own corner pixels the same way and ran them through the new transform. This corrected transform disagrees with the original 9-point affine transform by tens of meters in places -- e.g. it revealed the original trace had Blocks 3/4 shifted east into the excavation pit/street area, and Blocks 11/12 roughly 2x too deep -- and the new positions now land within real, distinct site features (buildings, graded lots) visible in satellite imagery rather than straddling roads. Known residual limitation: GCP street positions are centerline-based (matching OSM convention), while a block boundary should sit at the near curb, so any edge close to a GCP street can land a few meters into that street after transformation -- checked for and corrected on this block's street-facing edge(s) where applicable using this project's already-established grid bearing (356.5 deg) and, where available, an independently diagram-measured depth/width. Treat corrected vertex positions as accurate to roughly 10-15m (tighter than the original 8-24m transform, but still not survey-grade). RE-CORRECTED 2026-09-16 (same day, third pass): the independent per-block TPS re-trace (see above) still measured each block's own 4 corners in isolation, which -- despite using the same transform -- left small (3-12m) spurious gaps or misalignments at boundaries the diagram actually draws as shared or tightly-spaced between adjacent blocks (caught after the user pointed out the diagram itself has ~zero wasted space and specifically that the PG&E switchyard polygon sits directly against Block 5 in the diagram, not ~60m away as this dataset had it). Re-measured EVERY block's corners in a single consistent pass using programmatic black-pixel border detection (long contiguous runs = real borders, filtered from text/dimension-arrow strokes by requiring the run to span nearly the full block height/width), cross-validated with fine-pixel-gridline crops, so that shared or consistently-measured boundaries between neighboring blocks now come from the same underlying pixel measurements rather than independent eyeball estimates. Batch-transformed through the same GDAL/TPS fit as before. This pass also corrected several block extents that were measured imprecisely in the prior pass (e.g. Block 5's real stepped/notched south edge, Block 11's true position -- it does NOT sit flush against Block 15, there is real Power Station Park open space between them). GCP CORRECTION 2026-09-16 (fourth pass): user flagged that Block 8/12 should touch Delaware Street with park space between them, and that Block 3/4's shapes looked off -- investigation found the root cause was a single mis-measured ground control point. The 'Delaware St x Humboldt St' GCP used for the whole site's TPS transform had been placed at pixel (2227, 986), which is actually deep inside Building 9's own footprint in the diagram, not on Delaware Street at all -- confirmed by comparing pixel spacing between the three Humboldt-row GCPs (Maryland/Delaware/Georgia Lane): Maryland-to-Georgia-Lane's pixel:real-world ratio implied Delaware should sit at roughly pixel x=2020, not 2227, and a direct color-transition scan at y=986 confirmed the real street gap is at x=1994-2035. Corrected the GCP to (2015, 986) (same real-world coordinate, just the right pixel) and re-ran the TPS transform for the whole site. This produced large corrections concentrated exactly where the user's complaint pointed -- Block 4 shifted 33-60m, Block 3's east corners ~28-33m, Block 8's east corners ~29-31m, Block 12's east corners ~26-27m -- while blocks far from the error (5, 15, 7, 11, PG&E) shifted well under 5m, consistent with a localized GCP error rather than a global transform problem. 2026-09-29 accuracy audit: the source URL cited for this file (the August 22, 2019 public-review draft #2 of the D4D at default.sfplanning.org) is dead (404); the text above describes the final D4D (dated February 26, 2020), so source_doc_urls now points to potreropower_D4D_final.pdf, where Figure 6.2.3 Building Height Plan is on printed p.245 (PDF p.247) with a scale bar (0-400 ft), a north arrow and the street labels listed above. Corrections to statements above: the '~2023-24 arrival' of UCSF as anchor tenant has no cited source; the dated source found is the UC Regents' September 2024 CEQA findings (Attachment 6), which state that in 2024 the City approved an assignment and assumption agreement under which UCSF assumes a portion of the developer's rights. The Sophie Maxwell / UCSF Block 2 anchor and clip steps are this project's own work, not a source claim. The accuracy_caveat's 'vacant/graded land, unaddressed in the Assessor roll' was wrong: the block is in the PG&E-owned northern switchyard area and DataSF Parcels has an addressed lot (4175499, 1101 Illinois St) over it. Treat vertex positions as accurate to roughly 10-25m, not survey-grade, and treat the block's applicability itself as somewhat more provisional than Mission Rock's or Pier 70's equivalent entries. Rebuilt 2026-09-16 via GDAL GCP/TPS georeferencing -- see digitization_method. Re-measured 2026-09-16 (third pass) in a single consistent pixel-detection pass across the whole block layout -- see digitization_method. Re-corrected 2026-09-16 (fourth pass) after fixing a mis-measured GCP -- see digitization_method.'; notes: 'Approximate polygon for a real, D4D-adopted block (final D4D, Feb 26, 2020: Table 3.1.1 and Figure 6.2.3) -- see accuracy_caveat. DataSF Parcels lists an active lot with an address, 4175499 (1101 Illinois St, recorded 2024-10-15), covering nearly all of this approximate footprint; the dataset does not say whether that lot is the switchyard parcel. Traced from an adopted regulatory diagram, positioned by matching several points on it to real streets, but this diagram is dated 2020 and may not reflect later design changes (as already found for the UCSF/Sophie Maxwell area). properties.why_no_real_parcel: Block 13's land is not part of the developer-owned 21-acre Power Station parcel: it is in the 4.8-acre PG&E-owned northern switchyard (final D4D Figure 1.2.1; SF Planning project page), which the Master Plan includes but whose build-out depends on the switchyard's relocation and on the property coming within the Development Agreement's jurisdiction. DataSF Parcels lists an active lot, 4175499 (1101 Illinois St, recorded 2024-10-15), overlapping about 99% of this approximate footprint; whether it is PG&E's switchyard parcel is not established, so this uses hand-traced approximate geometry instead.
properties.regulatory_context: The D4D's Permitted Uses table (Table 3.1.1) shows Block 13 permits Residential, Institutional, Retail, Non-Retail Sales/Services (office), Entertainment and PDR uses (PDR limited to listed uses at the lower floors); Laboratory and Life Science are not permitted. Figure 6.2.3 of the final D4D gives Block 13 two height limits by its colour-coded labels, 85 ft and 125 ft; the '300'MAX' and '280'MAX' labels on the block sit on tick-ended dimension lines (plan extents of the 125 ft zone), not heights, and Standard 6.2.2 lists Block 13 among the midrise buildings (101-145 ft). The tallest limit on the site is Block 7's 240 ft. No construction-start source found.
properties.notes: Approximate polygon for a real, D4D-adopted block (final D4D, Feb 26, 2020: Table 3.1.1 and Figure 6.2.3) -- see the accuracy caveat. properties.regulatory_context: Flat 90 ft max height per Figure 6.2.3 (the block is labelled '14 90'' on the colour-coded plan). The final D4D's Table 3.1.1 (printed p.47) permits residential, institutional, retail and non-retail sales/services (office) uses on Block 14 and does not permit laboratory or life-science uses; recorded here as 'mixed' as a summary of that table, not a confirmed program. Block 14 is within the PG&E Sub-area: the D4D's Appendix E says redevelopment of that sub-area is subject to PG&E's long-range facilities planning and that portions of it 'may or may not ultimately be redeveloped', and SF Planning's project page says built-out of the PG&E lands depends on relocation of the switchyard; 'planned' reflects the D4D and the October 2020 Phase 1 approval (Phase 2), not a committed project.

The owner then specified translating fragment 9 (a separate paved path, ~7,932 sqm) north to merge with the truncated fragment 7, closing a real but narrow (~17-22m) planting-strip gap between the two rather than tracing that gap directly -- picked a 0.0002 deg (~22m) north shift, comfortably past the ~0.000156 deg (~17.3m) minimum needed for the two shapes to touch, for a clean overlapping seam rather than a knife-edge join.
